read.sections.0.heading.source: Belonging is more than being there
read.sections.0.heading.back: Belonging is more than just being there

read.sections.0.text.source: Belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. A person can sit in a room with a group and still feel ignored or left out. People can belong to many kinds of groups at once, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. It might also be people who share a language or a hobby. Many cultures value these connections. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. It is usually explained as “a person is a person through other people”. It means we grow as people through our relationships with others.
read.sections.0.text.back: Belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. A person may sit in the same room as a group but still feel ignored or left out. People can belong to many groups at the same time, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. A group may also be people who use the same language or share a hobby. Many cultures value this kind of connection. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu, which is often explained as "a person becomes a person because of other people", meaning we grow into people through our relationships with others.
read.sections.0.text.note: Ubuntu written อูบุนตู with (Ubuntu) once in each version, so the voice reads the Thai and readers see the original. The saying 'a person is a person through other people' is คนจะเป็นคนได้ก็เพราะคนอื่น: check it is clear and close enough.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Belonging means you feel accepted in a group. You feel connected to the people in it. A person can be in a room and still feel left out. People can belong to many groups. It can be a class, a team or friends. It can be people who share a language or a hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow as people through other people.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Belonging is feeling that a group accepts you. You feel connected to the people in the group. A person may be in the room but still feel left out. People can be part of many groups. It may be a class, a team or a group of friends. It may be people who use the same language or share a hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow into people because of others.

read.sections.1.text.source: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the youth club's feedback cards. One member finds meetings difficult when everyone speaks at once. Another member only joined after someone explained the rules quietly. The club does not need to change its members. Instead, it can change how it works. Turn-taking rules make meetings easier to follow, because only one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the club's routines to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can participate.
read.sections.1.text.back: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the youth club's feedback cards. One member finds meetings hard when everyone talks at once. Another member joined only after someone quietly explained the rules. The club doesn't need to change its members, but it can change its own way of working. A take-turns rule makes meetings easier to follow because one person speaks at a time. A welcome buddy can help explain the club's routine to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can take part.
read.sections.1.text.note: 'routine' is กิจวัตร (glossary word). It is mostly used for a person's daily routine; for a club's usual way of doing things a reviewer might prefer ขั้นตอนประจำ or ธรรมเนียมของชมรม. 'remove barriers' is เอาอุปสรรคออกไป (everyday) rather than ขจัดอุปสรรค (formal).

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A barrier makes it hard to take part. Read the club's cards. One person finds it hard when everyone talks at once. One person joined after someone explained the rules. The club does not need to change its members. It can change how it works. With turn-taking, one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the routines. Now more people can join in.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Barriers make it hard to join in. Read the club's cards. One person finds it hard when everyone talks at once. Another joined after someone explained the rules. The club doesn't have to change its members. The club can change how it works. If people take turns, one person speaks at a time. A welcome buddy can help explain the routine. Now more people can join in.

read.sections.2.heading.note: 'have a say' is the idiom มีสิทธิ์มีเสียง (usual spelling with ์), used throughout. 'rights' in the children's rights sentence is สิทธิ (KEY_TERMS). Check the two spellings side by side don't confuse learners.

read.sections.2.text.source: Belonging also grows when people have a real say. One card says: “I want to help choose the activities, not only attend them”. A student planning group gives members more agency, which means the power to make choices and act. The UN agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinions on things that affect them. It also says they can join or set up groups. A good group asks members what is working and what is not. Nobody should have to share private things about their life to belong.
read.sections.2.text.back: Belonging also grows when people really have a say. One card says, "I want to help choose activities, not just attend them." A student planning group gives members more agency, which means the power to choose and act. The United Nations agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinions on matters that affect them, and that children can join or form groups. A good group asks members what works and what doesn't. No one should have to share personal stories from their life in order to belong.
read.sections.2.text.note: 'The UN agreement on children's rights' is ข้อตกลงของสหประชาชาติว่าด้วยสิทธิเด็ก, keeping the English's plain 'agreement'. Its formal Thai name is อนุสัญญาว่าด้วยสิทธิเด็ก (used in the source label). 'agency' follows KEY_TERMS: พลังในการเลือกเอง (check).

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Belonging grows when people have a say. One member wants to help choose what the club does. A planning group gives members more agency. They can make choices and act. A UN agreement says children have a right to give their opinions. They can join groups or start them. A good group asks what works and what does not. No one has to share private things to belong.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Belonging grows when people have a say. One member wants to help choose what the club does. A planning group gives members more agency. They can choose and act. A United Nations agreement says children have the right to give opinions. Children can join groups or start their own. A good group asks what works and what doesn't. No one has to share personal stories to belong.

watch.summary.source: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they learn. Their identity grows from their experiences. These include goals they reached and mistakes they learned from. Belonging grows when adults know students' names. It also grows when students can share their work and not be judged. For them, agency means feeling sure that you can reach a goal if you work at it. Older helpers, friends and chances to lead can help. At the end, they tell adults that young people are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers share their own stories, but you do not need to share yours. You can think about the questions using the youth club, or a group you know.
watch.summary.back: In this video, youth talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they learn. Their identity grows from experience, including goals they achieved and mistakes they learned from. Belonging grows when adults know students' names, and also when students can share their work without being judged. For them, agency means confidence that you can reach your goals if you try. Older people who help, friends, and chances to lead all help. At the end, they tell adults that youth are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers tell their own stories, but you don't need to tell yours. You can think about these questions using the youth club or a group you know.
watch.summary.note: 'Older helpers' is คนที่โตกว่าซึ่งคอยช่วยเหลือ; a reviewer may prefer รุ่นพี่ or พี่เลี้ยง.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Please have a local educator review this lesson before use. Belonging can bring up feelings about home, family or loss for some learners.

sensitiveNotes.0.note: Sensitive notes for educators. 'Please have a local educator review' is ควรให้ผู้สอนในท้องถิ่นตรวจทาน... (no กรุณา, as the brief asks). Check the whole set reads with the right care for adults working with refugee youth.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Never ask learners to talk about their own home, family, past or times they did not belong. The youth club, a class, a team, a group of friends, a language or a hobby always work as examples.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Don't ask learners to talk about home, family, their past or times they didn't feel they belonged. The youth club, class, team, friends, languages or hobbies can always be used as examples.

sensitiveNotes.2.source: If a learner chooses to share something personal, listen calmly, thank them, and do not ask follow-up questions in front of the group. Follow your centre's safeguarding steps if you are worried.
sensitiveNotes.2.back: If a learner chooses to share something personal, listen calmly, thank them and don't ask further questions in front of the group. If you are worried, follow your centre's child safeguarding steps.
sensitiveNotes.2.note: 'follow-up questions in front of the group' shortened to อย่าถามต่อหน้ากลุ่ม (don't ask [more] in front of the group); 'safeguarding steps' is ขั้นตอนการคุ้มครองเด็ก.
